newsitem.title: UK: Second gene found for tuberous sclerosis.
newsitem.headline: Second gene found for tuberous sclerosis.

text.p: Researchers said on Friday they had found a second gene for tuberous sclerosis, a rare but unpleasant genetic condition that causes tumours all over the body.
About one in 6,000 babies are born with the condition, which can lead to epilepsy, learning difficulties, autism and kidney and skin disease.
A team of European and U.S. researchers said they had found a second gene that causes the condition, leading to hopes there could be a test for it.
The first gene, TSC2, was discovered in 1993 and accounts for half the cases of the disease. But researchers could not track down a second possible gene, dubed TSC1, despite 10 years of efforts.

But the international team from Erasumus University in Rotterdam, University College in London, the Whitehead Centre for Genome Research in Cambridge, Massachussetts, and other centres said they had finally found it.
Reporting in the journal Science, they said they had sequenced the gene -- identified every constituent amino acid -- as part of the Human Genome Project mapping the genes in the human body.

"At present we do not understand how either TSC1 or TSC2 work, but they certainly control the growth of tumours in these patients, and seem to form a previously unknown pathway of growth control which could be relevant to other tumours and to normal development," the researchers said in a statement.
Some sort of therapy could be found, they added.

"This is fantastic news," Stephen Stirk, chairman of the British-based Tuberculosis Sclerosis Association, said. "It is a significant breakthrough which will really make a difference to (sufferers') lives."
